cues.text: A Devotion That Became a Theft
In 1194, tradition holds, a woman in Augsburg was known for her deep devotion to the Blessed Sacrament.
She received Holy Communion and, without being noticed, kept the host rather than consuming it, wishing to have it in her own home for private adoration.
At a time when tabernacles were not yet common in parish churches, her longing, however disordered its expression, was not unusual for her era.
She wrapped the host between two pieces of wax and kept it hidden inside a cupboard in her home.
Five Years of a Troubled Conscience
The woman kept the host in this way for five years, tradition relates, until her conscience would no longer let the matter rest.
On May 11, 1199, she confessed what she had done to Father Berthold, superior of the Convent of the Holy Cross, who had her bring the hidden host back to the church.
Flesh, Growth, and a Bishop's Proclamation
When the wax covering was opened, the account holds, the host inside was found transformed: divided into two parts joined by what witnesses described as thin threads of bleeding flesh.
In the weeks that followed, from Easter Sunday to the Feast of St. John the Baptist, the host is said to have visibly grown and swollen until it cracked its wax casing entirely.

Bishop Udalskalk of Augsburg examined the reports and proclaimed the event a Eucharistic sign worthy of annual commemoration, and the relic was placed for public veneration, later housed in a crystal monstrance.
A Relic That Survived Centuries of Upheaval
The relic's history since has been anything but quiet.
It was hidden away during the early years of the Reformation after 1517, then brought back into public procession in 1537.
It was sent into a second hiding from 1538 to 1548, and its veneration was again disrupted under Swedish occupation in 1632 and French occupation around 1800.
On the night of February 25, 1944, Allied bombing destroyed much of the Church of the Holy Cross itself, though the relic survived.
Devotional sources describe repeated examinations of the relic across the centuries as having found it consistent with human tissue.
However, no single peer-reviewed scientific study of the kind conducted at Lanciano is known to have been published.
This claim should be received with that qualification.
Legacy
Few Eucharistic traditions carry within their own history such a clear record of survival against the currents of European history.
These included reformation, war, occupation, and finally aerial bombardment, each of which the community met by hiding, protecting, or restoring the same small relic rather than abandoning it.
Today the Church of the Holy Cross, cared for by the Dominican friars of Augsburg, still holds what devotion has called for over eight centuries the Wunderbarlichen Gutes , the "Miraculous Good."
We find in this long history less a single dramatic moment than a community's patient, repeated choice to keep faith with what it believed God had shown it.
This fidelity outlasted empires, armies, and the ordinary erosions of eight hundred years.
